n: Seeing the crowds, Jesus goes up a mountainside and sits down — the usual posture of a Jewish teacher. His disciples gather close. Like Moses giving the law on a mountain, Jesus gives His higher law. The resurrected Savior gave a similar sermon at the temple in Bountiful (3 Nephi 12–14).

f.w: he went up into a mountain

f.g: When He sat down — teachers sat to teach.

n: Jesus begins teaching. Chapters 5–7 are called the Sermon on the Mount.

f.g: A formal way of introducing a solemn teaching.

n: The first of the Beatitudes (“blessings”). Those who recognize their spiritual need are truly blessed — the kingdom is theirs. In 3 Nephi the Savior adds “who come unto me.”

f.g: Greek makarios — truly happy, favored by God.

n: Those who mourn — for sin, loss, or the world’s suffering — will be comforted by God.
The meek — gentle, humble, teachable — will inherit the earth, quoting Psalm 37. Meekness is strength under control, not weakness.
Those who hunger and thirst for righteousness will be filled. The Book of Mormon version adds “with the Holy Ghost.”
The merciful will receive mercy. How we treat others shapes how we will be treated.
The pure in heart — sincere, single-minded, clean — will see God. A promise Latter-day Saints take literally.
Peacemakers — those who actively make peace — will be called God’s children, because they act like Him.
Those persecuted for doing right are blessed; the kingdom of heaven is theirs.
Jesus applies it personally: you are blessed when people insult, persecute, and lie about you because of Me.

f.g: Insult, abuse verbally.

n: Rejoice and be glad, for your reward in heaven is great — they persecuted the prophets the same way. Joseph Smith received similar comfort.
You are the salt of the earth — preserving and adding flavor. But salt that loses its saltiness is useless. Disciples must stay true to be useful.

f.g: Flavor, taste.

n: You are the light of the world, like a city on a hill that can’t be hidden.

f.w: Ye are the light of the world

n: No one lights a lamp and covers it with a basket; they put it on a stand to light the whole house.

f.g: A small oil lamp.
A basket or measuring container.
Lampstand.

n: Let your light shine so others see your good works and glorify your Father in heaven. The goal is to point people to God, not ourselves.
Jesus hasn’t come to abolish the law of Moses or the prophets, but to fulfill them — to bring them to their full purpose in Himself.

f.w: I am not come to destroy, but to fulfil

n: Not even the smallest letter or stroke of the law will pass away until everything is fulfilled.

f.g: The Greek iota, the smallest letter — like the Hebrew yod.
A tiny stroke that distinguishes one Hebrew letter from another.

n: Whoever breaks even a small commandment and teaches others to, will be least in the kingdom; whoever keeps and teaches them will be great. Teachers carry extra responsibility.
Your righteousness must go beyond the scribes’ and Pharisees’ — beyond outward rule-keeping to a changed heart. In 3 Nephi, the Savior says instead “except ye shall keep my commandments.”

f.w: exceed the righteousness of the scribes and Pharisees

n: Now six contrasts: “You have heard… but I say.” The first: the old law says, “Don’t murder.”

f.g: The local court.

n: Jesus goes to the root: anger and contempt. Calling someone “Raca” (empty-head) or “fool” shows a heart that could lead to murder. The Book of Mormon and JST omit “without a cause,” making the standard even higher.

f.g: Absent from 3 Nephi 12:22 and the JST.
An Aramaic insult meaning “empty-headed.”
The Sanhedrin, the high Jewish court.
Literally “the Gehenna of fire” — named after a valley outside Jerusalem where trash burned.

n: So if you are offering a gift at the altar and remember someone has something against you —

f.g: An offering at the temple.
Anything.

n: — leave your gift, go make things right, then come back and offer it. Reconciliation with others comes before worship. In 3 Nephi: “come unto me with full purpose of heart.”

f.w: first be reconciled to thy brother

n: Settle disputes quickly while you can, before they end up in court and you go to prison.
You won’t get out until you pay the last penny. Unresolved wrongs carry a cost.

f.g: A tiny Roman coin; 3 Nephi 12:26 uses the Nephite “senine.”

n: Second contrast: the law says, “Don’t commit adultery.”
Jesus says lustful looking is already adultery in the heart. Purity begins with thoughts.

f.w: looketh on a woman to lust after her

n: If your eye causes you to sin, tear it out — better to lose one part than your whole self. This is hyperbole: deal decisively with whatever leads to sin.

f.g: Cause to stumble, lead into sin.
JST and 3 Nephi 12:29-30 explain it as not allowing these things to enter the heart; taking up one’s cross.

n: If your hand causes you to sin, cut it off. Remove what tempts you, even if it’s painful.

f.w: if thy right hand offend thee

n: Third contrast: the law allowed divorce with a written certificate.
Jesus raises the standard: divorce except for unfaithfulness leads to adultery. He restores God’s original intent for lasting marriage.

f.w: saving for the cause of fornication

f.g: Divorce.

n: Fourth contrast: the law said don’t break your oaths; keep your vows to the Lord.

f.g: Swear falsely; break an oath.

f.w: perform unto the Lord thine oaths

n: Jesus says don’t swear oaths at all — not by heaven, which is God’s throne.
Nor by the earth (His footstool) or Jerusalem (the great King’s city). People tried to make “lesser” oaths they could break; Jesus says everything belongs to God.

f.w: the city of the great King

n: Don’t even swear by your own head — you can’t make one hair white or black. We don’t control even ourselves.

f.w: thou canst not make one hair white or black
f.g: A reminder of how little we control.

n: Simply let your “yes” mean yes and your “no” mean no. Honesty shouldn’t need oaths.

f.g: Speech, words.
Or “from the evil one.”

n: Fifth contrast: the law of “an eye for an eye” limited revenge to fair punishment by courts.
Jesus says don’t retaliate. If someone slaps your right cheek — an insulting backhand — turn the other also. Respond to insult without revenge.

f.g: Don’t retaliate against an evil person.

f.w: turn to him the other also

n: If someone sues for your shirt, let them have your coat too — go beyond what’s demanded.

f.g: The inner tunic.
The outer robe, which the law said could not be kept overnight (Exodus 22:26-27).

n: If forced to carry something a mile — as Roman soldiers could require — go two. Turn compulsion into service.

f.w: compel thee to go a mile
f.g: Roman soldiers could legally force civilians to carry gear one mile.
Two.

n: Give to those who ask, and don’t turn away those who want to borrow. Generosity reflects God’s own giving.

f.w: Give to him that asketh thee

n: Sixth contrast: “Love your neighbor and hate your enemy.” The law commanded love of neighbor; “hate your enemy” was a popular addition.
Jesus commands: love your enemies, bless those who curse you, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who mistreat you. This is the heart of Christlike love.

f.g: Mistreat, insult.

n: Then you will be true children of your Father, who sends sun and rain on good and bad alike. Loving enemies makes us like God.

f.w: he maketh his sun to rise on the evil and on the good

n: If you love only those who love you, what reward is that? Even tax collectors do that.

f.g: Tax collectors for Rome, despised as collaborators and cheats.

n: If you greet only your own people, what are you doing beyond others? Disciples are called to more.

f.g: Greet warmly.

n: “Be ye therefore perfect, even as your Father which is in heaven is perfect.” The Greek suggests complete, whole, mature. After His resurrection Jesus said “even as I, or your Father” (3 Nephi 12:48). Perfection is a lifelong goal reached through Christ’s grace.

f.g: Greek teleios — complete, whole, fully developed.
